source.title: MESA: Improving MoE Safety Alignment via Decentralized Expertise
source.authors: Yi-Tong Sun; Yao Huang; Teng Li; Ran-Jie Duan; Yi-Chi Zhang; Xing-Jun Ma; Hui Xue; Xing-Xing Wei

page_placements.theme: Mixture-of-experts routing and expert selection mediate safety

record.tranche_reason: The study compares targeted expert masking with random masking to test whether MoE safety is concentrated in particular experts, using a different method from the claim's parameter- or rank-localization framing.
record.gate_note: The study tests expert-level safety concentration with inference-time masking. Its 30K mixed-data training results are not tests of harmful-only or benign-only fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred examples. Its router-exploitation attack is related to bypassing safety but is not a compliant-opening, suffix, or decoding-change test. Figure 5's expert-overlap results are not direct measurements of harmful-compliance behavior.
record.test_reason: Section 4.2.2 and Figure 4 compare masking of the highest-safety-activated experts with random masking on two MoE models. This tests whether safety is carried by a small subset of parameters (experts), bearing on V5 with a method different from the originals. The rest of the paper is a mitigation method (MESA) and its safety/utility benchmarks, which test no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also present safety sparsity in MoEs as a vulnerability. They claim MESA reaches state-of-the-art safety (e.g., Strata 90.90% on DeepSeek) while preserving utility, against global alignment methods that cost reasoning ability.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes architecture-aware MoE alignment using OT-based expert selection and routing refinement, with 30K mixed safety and helpfulness training data; it does not reproduce the original fine-tuning or token-depth methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Masking effects vary by model, benchmark, and masking strategy; MESA's selected expert ratio is w = 0.15 for DeepSeek and w = 0.1 for Qwen.

fits_no_version.finding: FSOUR routing-exploitation attack ASR on DeepSeek differs by alignment method: SFT/Stair-DPO/MESA 0%, SafeX 15.38%, GRPO 22.73%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Router-manipulation attacks bypass safety in some safety-tuned MoE models, depending on the alignment method.

fits_no_version.finding: Safety-related queries route through a narrow subset of experts, while general queries use a broad set (Section 2.2, Figure 7). This is an activation pattern, not a behaviour rate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In MoE LLMs, expert routing for harmful prompts is more concentrated than for general prompts.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The masking outcome is stated only in aggregate in the text and numerical results are in Figure 4; the textual account does not identify the combinations behind exceptions. Evaluation covers two MoE models and does not test weights or ranks directly.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 and the fine-tuning ablations report safety and utility for MESA and other methods but do not test the specified harmful-only or benign-only small-data fine-tuning claims. Figure 5 reports expert-overlap patterns, not direct harmful-compliance outcomes.

untested.parts: Localization in individual weights, neurons or low ranks; dense models; models beyond DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B.
Not tested: no harmful-only small-data fine-tuning.
Not tested: training mixes SafeRLHF safety data with UltraFeedback; there is no benign-only fine-tuning arm.
Not tested: no per-token KL measurement.
Not tested: no prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks; FSOUR manipulates routing.
Not tested: the authors only speculate that GRPO relies on shallow rejection heuristics.

missing.what: Per-model, per-method, per-benchmark safety scores under random versus Top-5/Top-10 targeted masking, including the unmasked baseline model rather than only SafeX/MESA.

record.verdict_notes: This is mainly a mitigation paper; only the masking analysis bears on V5, and it is reported in aggregate in the text. The record's state 'partial' is kept because the authors note exceptions. The expert-selection ablations (Table 3, ECmax) are about which experts to fine-tune, not localization tests. The paper cites one original source (2406.05946) but is not an original source itself.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-only fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred examples.
No ordinary-benign-only or carefully chosen benign-only fine-tuning test.
No per-token KL measurement between aligned and base models.
No compliant-opening prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change test.
Tests localization at the MoE expert level only; it does not measure individual weights or ranks, or test dense models.
Does not test why safety might be shallow or relate shallowness to training data or objective.
Does not train or evaluate safety spread across response-token positions.

relationships.condition: Qwen on Strata; DeepSeek on complex benchmarks; models tuned with decentralizing methods (MESA)
relationships.reason: On Qwen Strata, random masking also causes large drops. DeepSeek is robust on complex benchmarks. The authors say MESA-tuned models resist targeted masking, so concentration depends on the alignment method (R1, R2).
relationships.display_finding: Random masking also caused large drops on Qwen Strata, DeepSeek stayed robust on complex benchmarks, and the authors say MESA-tuned models resist targeted masking, so concentration depends on the alignment method.

reader_labels.condition: Expert masking across the tested MoE models and methods, as described in the text
reader_labels.reason: The authors report sharper safety declines from masking highly safety-activated experts than from random masking in most settings, consistent with expert-level concentration (R1, R2).
